did_you_know.text: Psalm 74 begins with the word “maskil” and the attribution “of Asaph.” It is written as a prayer of lament and questioning: Why has God abandoned his people?

The psalmist recalls Israel as the community God purchased and redeemed in the past, and Mount Zion as the place where God dwelled. In this way, he bases his plea on the relationship between the LORD and his people.
The description of the enemy in the temple includes tools used for cutting and destruction, indicating from the text that the holy place was violently destroyed and desecrated.

The psalmist describes the burning of the temple and the desecration of the dwelling place of God’s name. The destruction is presented not only as an attack on the people, but also as an assault on the temple and God’s honor.

One sign of the crisis is the absence of “our signs,” along with no prophet and no clear knowledge of how long the suffering will last. The verse expresses a sense of being without guidance and of God hiding his face.
In the middle of the psalm, the focus shifts from lament to remembrance: God is portrayed as King from ancient times and as the one who works salvation throughout the earth.

The psalmist describes God’s power over the sea and over “the heads of the sea monsters.” This is a poetic description of his control over the forces of the sea and chaos, not a detailed historical account.
God’s rule is also described through the order of creation: day and night, the heavenly lights, the boundaries of the earth, and the seasons—summer and winter.
The image “Do not hand over the life of your dove to the wild beasts” portrays the vulnerable people as prey, so the psalmist asks for protection for the poor and oppressed.
At the end, the psalmist calls on God, “Rise up... defend your cause.” He is asking not only for vengeance on behalf of the people, but also for protection of God’s name against the enemy’s insults.
